One Team. One Mission. No Limits.

We are Team Space Kitty, four teammates from Bangladesh, building Space Mission Tycoon for the Space Mission Design Game challenge

Who does what

Jafrin Alam Prima: team lead, strategy, research, data analysis 

Sabit Hasan Turzo: game mechanics & development

Md Tasrif Ibn Mizan: creative lead & game design

Afnan Mayeen Adib: project manager, video editor & story teller

In our game you don't fly the rocket. You run the agency and physics decides the rest 🚀
summary:
We developed Space Mission Tycoon, a multiplayer space-agency game where up to four friends run one space programme together, each in a different role. The Engineer designs and builds the rocket, the Scientist trains the crew and runs the tests, the Finance Manager chooses contracts and spends the budget, and the Safety Officer answers every emergency and gives the final GO for launch. Nobody can fly a mission alone, just like a real mission team. It also plays solo.

It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by putting a whole mission into one loop: take a contract, prepare the agency, design the rocket and payload part by part, launch, and see the result. Budget, mass, power, communications, schedule and risk all pull against each other, and the flight is simulated from the team's own design using the rocket equation. Real space weather from NASA's DONKI database can force a fly-or-wait decision.

It matters because students usually meet propulsion, power, communications and budgets as separate chapters, and rarely practise deciding as a team. Here they collide, and failure becomes the lesson: a mission ledger pinpoints the cause, such as "Delta-v 3.5 km/s, needed 9.0 km/s", and a learning screen explains how real programmes avoid it.
details:
A multiplayer game where friends design, launch and learn from space missions

In Space Mission Tycoon, up to four players run one space agency together. You never fly the rocket: you and your team make the decisions, and real rocket physics decides whether the mission succeeds.

Your agency's launch site, with staff, reputation, money and the deadline in the top bar.

Our unique feature: a mission team, not a solo player

Real missions are run by teams, where every specialist owns one part and nobody launches alone. Our game works the same way: up to four friends run one agency over Steam, each in a different role, and the rocket only flies when the team agrees.

The Team Play window: host over Steam, invite friends, pick roles and chat.

  • Engineer: designs and builds the rocket and payload, and picks the launch date.
  • Scientist: trains the crew and runs the engine, structure and communications tests.
  • Finance Manager: chooses contracts and spends the budget on facilities.
  • Safety Officer: answers every emergency and gives the final GO for launch.

The roles depend on each other. The Engineer needs money from the Finance Manager, the Finance Manager needs the Scientist's tests to raise contract pay, and the Safety Officer decides how much risk everyone carries to the pad. Everyone shares one clock, one budget and one rocket. It also plays solo, or with two or three.

Launch, then learn together. When the team launches, the flight is simulated from the rocket they built. Then the game's mission analysis reviews the whole run, every role's decisions included: the design, the tests, the budget and the risks taken. It grades the mission, pinpoints the cause of any failure and tells the team what to change before the next launch.

What you do

  1. Take a contract: a client sets the target, payload, budget, mass limit and deadline.
  2. Prepare: build facilities, train staff and test hardware.
  3. Design: build the rocket and its payload part by part.
  4. Launch: pick a date and watch a flight simulated from your own design.
  5. Learn: get the result, its cause, a grade and a lesson.

Every game starts by founding an agency.

One real mission, start to finish

A client offers the Polar Ice Survey: a radar satellite for a polar orbit, due in five months. The launch stays locked until the engines and the radio link are tested, because real agencies don't fly untested hardware either.

Each contract becomes the steps of a real mission.

Halfway through, the client asks for extra pilot training: accept for +$36M and more trust, or decline and lose trust.

Every decision card lists what you gain and what you lose.

We built Rocket 2: one stage, 14 m tall, 10 t at liftoff. The designer warned us: “Cannot reach space yet.” We launched anyway, the way a new player would.

The Rocket Designer: every stat updates with every part.

Liftoff.

Climbing on a single stage.

Out of delta-v.

Its thrust-to-weight ratio of 7.30 threw it off the pad, but it carried only 3.5 km/s of delta-v against the 9.0 km/s needed for orbit.

The mission ledger, with the line that decided it in red.

The learning outcome: 68/100, with real-world lessons.

The mission ledger shows the cause in one red line. The learning screen grades the mission 68/100 and gives the lesson real engineers learned the same way: a delta-v shortfall ends in orbit-less flights, which is why rockets have stages. So the next rocket gets a second stage.

How it works

  • Real physics in the code: Δv = Isp × g₀ × ln(m₀ / m₁) for every stage, thrust-to-weight to leave the pad, propellant flow, and staging with sea-level and vacuum engines.
  • 12 missions: from a university cubesat to a lander on Mars, with requirements for power, data rate and landing.
  • Two designers: more than 50 rocket parts, plus payloads with solar panels, batteries and antennas. A simple mode helps beginners.
  • A space centre to manage: six facilities compete for five plots, all limited by the power grid.
  • Risk you choose: tests, training and random events all change the chance of failure, and every choice shows its benefit, cost and risk first.
  • Rule-based analysis: the learning outcome uses fixed rules from real rocketry, so it never invents a cause.

The Payload Designer: power made against power used.

Choosing the launch date against the deadline.

NASA data in the game

Space weather is a real risk: in February 2022 a geomagnetic storm led SpaceX to lose up to 40 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites.

Space Mission Tycoon pulls live data from NASA's DONKI space-weather database through api.nasa.gov. Real coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms arrive as fly-or-wait decision cards, with added risk for any satellite launched through them. In team play, that call belongs to the Safety Officer. DONKI recorded a storm on 4 October 2026 that reached Kp 5.67, exactly the kind of event that should hold a launch.

Next in line, all tested and returning live data today: NASA POWER (wind and sunlight at our Dhaka launch site), EONET (Bay of Bengal cyclones), JPL Horizons (real Moon and Mars positions), NeoWs (asteroid contracts) and EPIC (whole-Earth photos).

Why it matters

Students usually meet propulsion, power, communications and budgets as separate chapters, and rarely practise deciding as a team. Here they meet all at once. The game answers the challenge with a complete mission loop, consequences on every decision, limited money, mass, power and time, a launch vehicle players build instead of pick, four-player teams with different responsibilities, and feedback that explains why a mission failed. We built it for classrooms, space clubs and groups of friends.

Next steps

  • Instruments and data: science instruments with a data budget sent home through the antenna.
  • Orbit choice: low, sun-synchronous, polar and geostationary orbits, with their effects.
  • More roles: an Astronaut for crewed contracts and a Communications Officer.
  • From game to GMAT: export a mission to NASA's open-source General Mission Analysis Tool.
  • An AI mission coach that writes the learning outcome from the ledger's own numbers.

Scope of this version: the flight model is built for learning, not flight certification. Contracts are fictional scenarios modelled on real mission types, and the orbit comes with the contract.

Tools and technologies

  • Game: Unity 6 and C#, with PurrNet networking over Steam
  • Art: Blender, Blockbench and Photoshop
  • Video: CapCut and DaVinci Resolve
  • AI assistants: Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, for research, writing and code help; reviewed and tested by the team

Team Space Kitty

  • Jafrin Alam Prima: team lead; strategy, research, data analysis
  • Sabit Hasan Turzo: game mechanics and development
  • Md Tasrif Ibn Mizan: creative lead and game design
  • Afnan Mayeen Adib: project manager, video editor and story teller
